title: Pre-Suasion by Robert Cialdini - Summary & Review (ANIMATED)
transcript: Robert Cialdini is one of the world's leading experts in the field of influence psychology. His fascinating book "Influence" came out 35 years ago, but it is still on the bookshelves of the most influential and successful people in the world. And while Influence deals with "persuasion," the art and science of getting someone to say "YES," Cialdini's new book is about PRE-persuasion: the process of organizing recipients to be receptive to a message BEFORE they encounter it. It is essentially the psychological framework in which you deliver your message. And that framework matters. A lot. Cialdini spent years studying the best salespeople, marketers, negotiators, and public speakers, and what he noticed was that the best performers spent more time crafting what they do and say before making a request than on the request itself. PRE-suasion offers a set of very practical ways to make people more receptive to your message, request, or proposal even before you deliver it to them. Just consider this example from the book: a consultant friend of the author was having trouble with prospects asking for discounts and challenging his rates when he was doing his pitch. One day, the consultant finished the joke, "As you can see, I'm not going to be able to charge you a million dollars for this," before stating his price. After this casual joke, no one challenged his $75,000 consulting fee. So, he made it a permanent part of his sales presentation and was never challenged again. What he found, by chance, was the powerful concept of "price anchoring". Mentioning a million dollars, even as a joke, made his $75,000 fee seem insignificant in comparison. By bringing forward his perspectives, he practically eliminated a major objection. How can YOU use these powerful tactics? 1) Attention When you pay attention to something, it will automatically become more important to you, or at least it will seem that way. The mainstream media take advantage of that on a daily basis. Experts believe that the media does not directly change people's opinions. But what they can do is change which story or topic receives more attention. They control what is being said. And when something or someone gets a lot of coverage, people assume it's important. The lesson here is: attention = importance. If you want to persuade someone of anything, you need to be able to capture, hold, and direct their attention. Cialdini offers 4 tactics that can transform you into a master of attention: 1) How to change the direction of someone's attention. In the most trivial argument you may have at work or at home, you are trying to convince someone by giving them reasons. But that's typically the hardest way to change someone's mind... as we've all experienced. A much easier and more powerful tactic is to change what that person is paying attention to. Since attention is limited and you can usually only focus on one thing at a time, when something new comes up, you almost immediately abandon the old thing. You can see this tactic in use by many politicians. When asked about the negative impact of a construction project, for example, they almost never argue, but change the narrative by talking about the new jobs created or the economic effect it will have on the neighborhood. By shifting the focus, they can also change the way people view the given project. 2) How to ask the "right" questions Using specific questions is a powerful way to direct attention to where it is needed. In a Canadian study, people were asked one of two questions: Are you "happy" with your social life or are you "unhappy" with your social life? Although the questions may seem identical to most, the results are nothing short of surprising. People who were asked if they were unhappy were 375% more likely to say yes. The way the question was phrased made some people think about their happiness and others about their unhappiness, hence the big difference in the results. REMEMBER: Questions are an extremely powerful way to guide someone's attention. 3) How to get attention Before you can direct someone's attention, you must first be able to capture it. How do you do that? Using time-tested attention testers: SEX The main reason you see models on magazine covers and in advertisements. Attractive people make you notice things, and while you're looking, you also notice the headlines, the products, and everything else. DANGER: a tactic similar to sex, but with the opposite message. Dangers and threats are attention magnets that the health industry is making very powerful use of. NOVELTY: For something to be noticed, it must stand out, be different, be new. If you're going to receive junk mail in a bright pink envelope, chances are you'll open it (at least the first time). In the sea of ​​letters, while, it will stand out demanding your attention. Once you have captured that valuable attention, how can you retain it? By using the most interesting person in the world for each person: themselves. Talking about the other person using "YOU" instead of "people" or "they" will make them pay attention. Or, speaking of its qualities and characteristics. That's why you hear many commercials using language like "in your 40s and overweight" or "you're a 50-year-old man struggling to find X." Make the other person the topic of conversation, and they'll pay attention to it almost indefinitely. So far you've become a master of attention, what's the next step in pre-persuasion? Cialdini calls for "unity". The feeling of being part of something bigger than yourself. It can be a shared group, a shared identity, or even a shared worldview. When a sports team wins or loses, its fans don't say "the team lost" or "they lost," they usually say "we lost." Similarly, religious people tend to refer to their churches as "our church". And, of course, the greatest unit of all: a family. There is nothing more united than a family, and that is why there are so many advertisements cleverly using language associated with family. The lesson here is to use language and actions to make people feel that they are part of something bigger, and that you are one of them. Invoke unity and you can influence them more powerfully. The final part of pre-persuasion is "connections". If you can design new or different mention connections, you can influence people more easily. Almost all large companies use this powerful tactic as part of their branding. That's why when you think of Mercedes Benz, you think of luxury, and when you think of Wal-Mart, you think of convenience and low prices. These associations have been carefully created by forging connections in your mind. This is usually done by showing them a scenario of some kind, or an attractive model or a well-known celebrity, and then linking the product or company simply by showing it. Just look at the next advertisement you see and you will notice nothing more than a background and a product image that often have nothing to do with each other, but create a powerful and subtle connection in your mind. Connections are also formed by being specific with the language and the words you use. Presenting something as an investment will have a connection versus presenting the cost of the exact same thing. And finally, use connections to build self-confidence. Cialdini followed a successful home alarm salesman. In the middle of his home presentation, he hit his forehead and said yes. I forgot something important in the car. Then he would ask the million-dollar question: "I don't want to interrupt your presentation, do you mind if I step outside and come back inside your house?" It's extremely subtle, but when you break it down, it's very powerful. Who do you let come and go from your house on their own? Only someone you trust, of course, a close friend or a family member. By evoking that mental connection, the salesperson was becoming much more trustworthy and, as a result, it was easier to close the sale. Let's sum it all up: the next time you want to persuade someone to keep these 3 things in mind: Attention: where is it going and can they hold it? Unit: Are you part of the team or are you part of them? Can you prove that? Connections: What positive mental connections and associations are you making? Now, let's see how you can make use of all these powerful tactics in your life.
